title: Anthropic in the Enterprise — Alexander Bricken & Joe Bayley

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The central theme is evals-first development methodology, evaluation design, and testing best practices drawn from hundreds of customer interactions. The Intercom Finn 2 case study grounds customer support, enterprise workflows are discussed throughout, and Anthropic's API and cloud partnerships serve as developer platform infrastructure. The talk covers deployment options, evaluation methodology, and optimization trade-offs including prompt caching and fine-tuning decisions. Assumes familiarity with LLM APIs, evaluation concepts, and enterprise deployment but remains accessible to practitioners. Recorded conference talk from the AI Engineer Summit 2025 Leadership Track. All claims are directly said in the transcript with anchored evidence IDs.

summary: Alexander Bricken and Joe Bayley from Anthropic present on enterprise AI implementation best practices drawn from hundreds of customer interactions. Bricken works on the Applied AI Product Engineering team focused on financial services technical implementation, while Bayley works on go-to-market, having joined over a year ago and observed model evolution from 2.1 to current capabilities. They describe Anthropic as an AI safety and research company building frontier models, with Sonet 3.5 leading coding evaluations like SWE-bench. A key differentiator is interpretability research—reverse-engineering models to understand feature activations, detect behaviors, and steer outputs, illustrated by the Golden Gate Claude example. They emphasize interpretability is still early stage, roughly the first 25% of a longer research timeline. On customer engagement, they encourage moving beyond chatbots and summarization toward transformative use cases like dynamically personalized learning platforms. Customers in tax, legal, and project management are achieving business-critical AI workflows. Anthropic offers deployment via API, Claude for Work, and cloud partnerships (AWS Bedrock, GCP Vertex) with equal support. The Applied AI team embeds with customers running sprints covering architecture, evals, prompt optimization, and AB testing. An Intercom case study details a two-month sprint optimizing prompts for their AI agent Finn, resulting in Finn 2 solving up to 86% of customer support volume with 51% out-of-the-box performance, plus improved tone adjustment and policy awareness. The presenters then share field best practices: evals should be designed before or shortly after workflows, not as an afterthought, and should include representative and edge-case test cases. They frame use case optimization as navigating a latent space to find attractor states, with evals serving as intellectual property for competitive advantage. On metrics, they describe an intelligence-cost-latency triangle where trade-offs must be defined in advance based on use case time sensitivity—customer support needs sub-10-second responses while financial research can tolerate minutes. They caution against premature fine-tuning, calling it 'brain surgery on the model' that can degrade reasoning in other domains; teams should exhaust alternatives like prompt engineering, prompt caching (90% cost reduction, 50% speed increase), contextual retrieval, and agentic architectures first.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Backgrounds
sections.summary: Alexander Bricken introduces himself as part of Anthropic's Applied AI team doing technical implementation and feeding insights back to research. Joe Bayley introduces himself from the go-to-market team, noting he joined over a year ago and has seen models evolve from 2.1 to current capabilities. They frame the talk around best practices and common mistakes from hundreds of customer interactions.

sections.title: Anthropic Mission and Sonet 3.5 Model
sections.summary: Anthropic is described as an AI safety and research company founded by leading experts, releasing frontier models with bleeding-edge safety techniques. Sonet 3.5 launched in late October, leads SWE-bench agentic coding evaluation leaderboard.

sections.title: Interpretability Research and Model Steering
sections.summary: Bricken explains interpretability as reverse-engineering models to understand thinking, currently at roughly 25% of a longer research timeline. Stages include understanding, detection, steering, and explainability. He describes feature activations (e.g., feature 304 for famous NBA players) and the Golden Gate Claude steering example. References monosemanticity and scaling monosemanticity papers.

sections.title: Customer Use Cases and Moving Beyond Chatbots
sections.summary: Bayley encourages customers to focus on core problems and move beyond chatbots/summarization toward transformative bets. Example: an onboarding/upskilling platform could hyper-personalize content, adapt difficulty dynamically, and update materials based on learning styles. Customers in tax, legal, and project management achieve high-quality, trustworthy AI workflows.

sections.title: Anthropic Product Offerings and Cloud Partnerships
sections.summary: Products include the API for embedding AI in products/services, Claude for Work for organizational use, and cloud partnerships with AWS Bedrock and GCP Vertex. Support is equal regardless of first-party or third-party access. Cloud deployment allows using existing infrastructure without managing new systems.

sections.title: Applied AI Team Engagement Model
sections.summary: Bricken describes the Applied AI team's role at the intersection of product research, customer interaction, and internal research. They support architecture, evals, prompt optimization, and deploy iterative loops into AB test environments. References published work including Barry's research paper and the Model Context Protocol. The team embeds with customers using Claude heavily who face niche challenges.

sections.title: Intercom Case Study and Finn 2 Results
sections.summary: Bayley describes Intercom's AI agent Finn as a leading customer service platform. Anthropic ran a two-month sprint optimizing prompts, after which Anthropic outperformed the previous LLM. Finn 2 launched, solving up to 86% of customer support volume with 51% out-of-the-box performance. Intercom uses resolution-based pricing, incentivizing helpfulness over deflection. Claude enabled tone adjustment, answer length control, and policy awareness capabilities. Bayley also notes Claude appearing as a therapist on Twitter as an entertaining character expression.

sections.title: Best Practices: Testing and Evaluation
sections.summary: Bayley identifies common evaluation mistakes: building workflows first then adding evals afterward, trusting vibes over representative samples, and not testing enough edge cases. He frames use case optimization as navigating a latent space between attractor states, where only empirical evaluations reveal outcomes. He tells customers evals are their intellectual property for competitive advantage. Best practices include setting up telemetry, backtesting, and including silly or unexpected test cases in eval sets.

sections.title: Best Practices: Identifying Metrics and Trade-offs
sections.summary: Organizations face an intelligence-cost-latency triangle of trade-offs and should define their balance in advance based on use case. Customer support needs sub-10-second responses or customers log off; financial research can tolerate 10 minutes because the capital allocation decision is high-stakes. UX techniques like thinking boxes or redirecting to other pages can mitigate perceived latency. More instruction sets may improve performance but increase latency.

sections.title: Best Practices: Fine-Tuning and Alternative Approaches
sections.summary: Bricken cautions against premature fine-tuning, calling it 'brain surgery on the model' that can limit reasoning in other domains. Teams should establish evals and clear success criteria first, try other approaches, and only fine-tune when alternatives fall short. Alternatives include prompt engineering, prompt caching (90% cost reduction, 50% speed increase), contextual retrieval, citations, and agentic architectures. Colleague Barry will speak tomorrow on agentic architectures. They close by inviting follow-up questions at the theater level lounge.
